check.why: The lesson presents both sides: taxes and tone changed, but the biggest programs and overall spending did not.

lessons.title: The Cold War Ends
lessons.mainIdea: Between 1985 and 1991 the Cold War ended without a shot fired between the superpowers, through American pressure, Soviet reform and the choices of ordinary people in Eastern Europe.
reading: In 1983 the Cold War felt as dangerous as it had in 1962. Reagan called the Soviet Union an evil empire and proposed a space-based missile shield the press named Star Wars. In September a Soviet fighter shot down a Korean airliner, killing everyone aboard. That November, a NATO exercise called Able Archer was so realistic that some Soviet officers feared it was cover for a real attack. Yet the year before, about a million people had rallied in New York's Central Park for a freeze on nuclear weapons, the largest protest in American history to that point. Public fear and a new Soviet leader would change the decade's direction.

Mikhail Gorbachev took power in March 1985 and launched *glasnost*, openness, and *perestroika*, restructuring, to save a Soviet economy that could not feed itself or match American spending. He and Reagan met four times. In December 1987 they signed the *INF Treaty*, the first agreement to eliminate an entire class of nuclear missiles. Earlier that year, standing at the Berlin Wall, Reagan had challenged Gorbachev, in words this book paraphrases, to open the gate and tear down the wall. The Soviet war in Afghanistan, begun in 1979, was draining money and lives, and the 1986 Chernobyl nuclear disaster exposed how much the system hid.

The end came from below. In June 1989 the Polish union *Solidarity* won free elections. Hungary opened its border to the West. On the night of November 9, 1989, after a confused East German announcement, crowds surged to the Berlin Wall and guards, with no orders to shoot, opened the gates. Within weeks Czechoslovakia's communist government fell peacefully. Germany reunited in October 1990. A coup by hard-liners in Moscow failed in August 1991, and on December 25, 1991, the Soviet flag came down over the Kremlin. In between, in early 1991, the United States led a coalition that drove Iraq's army out of Kuwait in a ground war of about one hundred hours, the first test of the new order.

Who ended the Cold War? One argument credits Reagan's military buildup, which the Soviets could not match. Another credits Gorbachev, who refused to send tanks as earlier leaders had in 1956 and 1968. A third credits the people in the streets of Warsaw, Leipzig and Prague. A fourth points to decades of economic failure that made collapse a matter of time. Historians weigh all four with the archives now open in Moscow. At home, the *peace dividend* had a local cost: Congress closed dozens of bases, including Chanute Air Force Base in Rantoul, Illinois, and Fort Sheridan north of Chicago, both shut in 1993.

words.d: Gorbachev's policy of openness, allowing more free speech and honest news in the Soviet Union
Gorbachev's restructuring of the Soviet economy and government after 1985
the 1987 U.S.-Soviet treaty that eliminated all intermediate-range nuclear missiles
the Polish independent trade union whose 1989 election victory began the fall of communism in Eastern Europe
money freed for other uses when military spending fell after the Cold War

look.title: Night at the Wall
look.text: November 9, 1989, near midnight, Bornholmer Street crossing, East Berlin. Thousands of people press against a gate that has been closed for twenty-eight years. The guards have a few dozen rifles and no instructions; their phone calls to headquarters go unanswered. A West Berlin crowd on the other side chants. A lieutenant colonel looks at the faces, then at his men, and orders the barrier raised.
look.prompt: The officer could have followed the old rules and waited. What made this moment different from 1956 in Hungary or 1968 in Prague, when Soviet tanks rolled?

check.q: What made the INF Treaty of 1987 a first?
choices: It eliminated an entire class of nuclear missiles rather than limiting their number
It ended the Soviet war in Afghanistan
It reunited Germany
It created NATO
check.why: Earlier treaties capped weapons; the INF Treaty removed intermediate-range missiles entirely.

check.q: Why does the lesson say the end of the Cold War came from below?
choices: Because Reagan ordered the wall opened
Because elections in Poland, open borders in Hungary and crowds at the Berlin Wall forced change before governments decided
Because Soviet tanks crushed the protests
Because the United Nations voted to end it
check.why: Ordinary people in Eastern Europe acted first, and Gorbachev chose not to send tanks.

check.q: Which evidence would best test the claim that Reagan's buildup ended the Cold War?
choices: The number of Reagan's television speeches
American election results from 1984
Soviet archives showing what its leaders thought they could afford
The height of the Berlin Wall
check.why: The claim is about Soviet decisions, so Soviet records are the evidence that could confirm or challenge it.

lessons.title: The Nineties and the Internet
lessons.mainIdea: The 1990s brought a long economic expansion, a budget surplus, bitter partisan fights and a new network, built in part in Illinois, that changed daily life.
reading: Bill Clinton won in 1992 by running on the economy while a Texas businessman, Ross Perot, took nearly a fifth of the vote as an independent. Clinton raised taxes on high earners to shrink the deficit and signed *NAFTA*, which removed most trade barriers with Canada and Mexico in 1994; unions warned it would send factories south, and supporters promised cheaper goods and new markets. In 1994 Republicans led by Newt Gingrich won the House for the first time in forty years. Two government shutdowns followed in 1995 and 1996. Clinton then signed a Republican welfare reform bill that set time limits on cash aid. By 1998 the budget was in *surplus* for the first time since 1969, and by 2000 unemployment was down to four percent. In December 1998 the House impeached Clinton for lying under oath about an affair; the Senate acquitted him.

Beneath the politics, a network was growing. The Defense Department had linked a few university computers in 1969. In 1991 a British scientist, Tim Berners-Lee, released the World Wide Web, a way to link documents across that network. It stayed a tool for scientists until 1993, when a team of students and staff at the National Center for Supercomputing Applications at the University of Illinois in Urbana released Mosaic, the first popular *browser* that showed pictures and text on the same page and worked with a mouse click. Two of its creators, Marc Andreessen and Eric Bina, left to found Netscape in 1994. Amazon opened in 1995, Google in 1998. In 1995 about one American adult in seven used the internet; by 2000 it was half.

Money poured in. Companies with no profits sold shares for billions, and the NASDAQ stock index, heavy with technology firms, roughly doubled in 1999 alone. In March 2000 the *dot-com bubble* burst, and the index lost about three quarters of its value over the next two and a half years. Yet the cables and the habits stayed. Meanwhile, the decade's prosperity was uneven. Factory employment kept falling, wages for workers without college degrees barely rose, and *globalization*, the tightening links of trade and money across borders, brought cheap electronics and lost jobs to the same towns. Chicago's downtown boomed while the old mill neighborhoods on the Southeast Side did not.

How should historians read the 1990s? One view calls it a golden decade: peace, surplus, falling crime, the web. Another sees a bubble in stocks and in confidence that popped in 2000 and 2001. A third asks whose decade it was, using Congressional Budget Office data showing that the top one percent's share of income rose steadily. The internet's early promise was that anyone could publish and everyone could know; later chapters of this story test that promise. To judge, compare the 1995 and 2000 adoption numbers with what people actually did online, then and now.

lessons.title: September 11
lessons.mainIdea: On September 11, 2001, nineteen al-Qaeda hijackers killed nearly three thousand people in under two hours, and the attacks reshaped American law, war and daily life.
reading: At 8:46 on a clear Tuesday morning, American Airlines Flight 11 struck the North Tower of the World Trade Center in New York. At 9:03 a second plane hit the South Tower, and millions watching live understood it was no accident. At 9:37 a third plane hit the Pentagon outside Washington. On the fourth, United Flight 93, passengers who had learned by phone what was happening fought the hijackers, and the plane crashed in a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, at 10:03. The South Tower fell at 9:59, the North at 10:28. Nearly three thousand people died, including 343 New York City firefighters who had climbed into the towers. The nineteen hijackers belonged to *al-Qaeda*, a network led by Osama bin Laden and sheltered by the Taliban government of Afghanistan, which had bombed two American embassies in 1998 and a Navy ship in 2000.

Every civilian plane in the country was grounded for days. In Chicago the Sears Tower was evacuated and the skies over O'Hare went silent. Blood banks had lines around the block. On September 18 Congress authorized the president to use force against those responsible; only one member voted no. President George W. Bush's approval rating rose to about ninety percent, and trust in government briefly reached levels not seen since the 1960s. At the same time, attacks on Muslims, Sikhs and Arab Americans spiked. Bush visited a Washington mosque six days after the attacks to say, in a paraphrase, that Islam was a religion of peace and that those who harassed Muslim Americans did not represent the country.

The legal changes came fast. The *Patriot Act*, signed in October 2001, expanded the government's power to conduct *surveillance*, share intelligence and track money. The *Department of Homeland Security*, created in 2002, combined twenty-two agencies, including a new one to screen airline passengers. A prison opened at the Guantanamo Bay naval base in Cuba in 2002 to hold suspects outside ordinary courts. The *9/11 Commission*, a bipartisan body, reported in 2004 that the FBI and CIA had each held pieces of the plot but had not shared them, and Congress created a Director of National Intelligence. Later revelations, in 2005 and again in 2013, showed the government had collected Americans' phone and internet records on a scale few had imagined.

For a student born after 2001, this is history, and it comes with the usual problems of evidence. The Commission's report is a federal document, public and searchable. Thousands of oral histories, from firefighters to office workers, are preserved in New York. The hardest questions are about trade-offs: how much privacy for how much safety, and who decides. Those questions did not begin on September 11, but that morning changed the answers a majority of Americans were willing to accept.

lessons.title: The Wars That Followed
lessons.mainIdea: The United States fought in Afghanistan for twenty years and in Iraq for nearly nine, wars that cost trillions of dollars and thousands of lives and whose results are still debated.
reading: American and allied forces attacked Afghanistan on October 7, 2001. The Taliban government fell within weeks, but bin Laden escaped across the mountains into Pakistan. What began as a hunt became a twenty-year effort to build a government, train an army and fight a Taliban that never went away. Navy SEALs killed bin Laden in Pakistan on May 2, 2011. The last American troops left in August 2021, and the Taliban retook the capital before they were gone. About 2,400 American service members died in Afghanistan, along with far larger numbers of Afghans. It was the longest war in American history.

Iraq was a choice. The Bush administration argued for *preemption*: striking a threat before it struck. Officials said Iraq held *weapons of mass destruction* and had ties to al-Qaeda. Congress authorized force in October 2002; that month a state senator named Barack Obama told a Chicago rally he opposed what he called a dumb war. The invasion began March 20, 2003, and Baghdad fell in three weeks. No banned weapons were ever found; a government inspection team said so in 2004. An *insurgency* and a civil war between Sunni and Shia Iraqis followed, and photographs of American guards abusing prisoners at Abu Ghraib shocked the world. A *surge* of troops in 2007 reduced the violence. Combat forces left in December 2011; the Islamic State seized much of Iraq in 2014 and drew Americans back. About 4,500 Americans died in Iraq. Estimates of Iraqi deaths start above a hundred thousand.

At home the wars were fought by a small share of the country. There was no draft; fewer than one percent of Americans served, and National Guard units, including Illinois brigades, deployed repeatedly. Hundreds of thousands of *veterans* came home with brain injuries or post-traumatic stress, and their care will cost the government for decades. The Senate reported in 2014 that the CIA had tortured prisoners, including by waterboarding, and argued it produced little useful intelligence; defenders disputed that. Researchers who add up the spending, the borrowing and the future care estimate the post-9/11 wars will cost trillions of dollars.

How should a student judge these wars? Start with what was claimed in 2002 and 2003 and set it beside what was known then and learned later. Read the 2002 debate in Congress, where the arguments on both sides are recorded. Count the costs in lives and dollars, and ask what the alternatives were. Then notice that a law passed in three days in September 2001 has been cited for military action in many countries for more than twenty years, and ask who should decide when a war ends.

lessons.title: The Crash of 2008
lessons.mainIdea: A housing bubble built on risky mortgages and complex financial bets burst in 2008, causing the worst downturn since the Depression and a fierce argument over bailouts.
reading: From 2000 to 2006 the price of an average American house roughly doubled. Lenders, confident prices would keep rising, offered *subprime mortgages* to borrowers with weak credit, often with low starting payments that jumped after two years. Banks did not keep these loans. Through *securitization* they bundled thousands of mortgages into bonds and sold them to investors around the world, and rating agencies stamped many of the bundles as safe as government debt. Other firms sold insurance on those bonds without setting money aside to pay claims. The whole structure assumed that home prices in Chicago, Phoenix and Miami could not all fall at once.

They did. Prices began sliding in 2006, payments jumped, and *foreclosure* notices spread through neighborhoods, hitting Black and Latino families, who had been steered toward the riskiest loans, hardest. In March 2008 the investment bank Bear Stearns collapsed and was sold with government help. On September 15, 2008, Lehman Brothers filed the largest bankruptcy in American history and no rescue came. The next day the government lent eighty-five billion dollars to the insurer AIG to keep it from failing. Credit froze: banks stopped lending even to each other. On September 29 the House voted down a rescue plan and the Dow fell 777 points in a day. Four days later Congress passed *TARP*, a seven-hundred-billion-dollar *bailout* that bought stakes in banks and later rescued General Motors and Chrysler.

The *Great Recession* officially ran from December 2007 to June 2009, but the damage lasted longer. The economy lost nearly nine million jobs, and unemployment reached ten percent in October 2009. Millions of families lost homes. In February 2009 Congress passed a stimulus of about eight hundred billion dollars in spending and tax cuts, and the Federal Reserve held interest rates near zero for seven years. Anger ran in two directions. On February 19, 2009, a television reporter on the floor of the Chicago Mercantile Exchange denounced help for struggling borrowers, a rant credited with sparking the Tea Party movement. In 2011 Occupy Wall Street protested the rescue of banks whose executives were never prosecuted. Congress passed the Dodd-Frank Act in 2010 to tighten rules on lenders.

Whose fault was it? The Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission, a federal body, concluded in 2011 that the crisis was avoidable and blamed regulators, lenders and the rating agencies; dissenting members blamed government housing policy and a global glut of savings. Was the bailout right? Defenders say it prevented a second Great Depression at a profit to taxpayers; critics say it saved the people who caused the crisis while homeowners got little. To weigh these, compare the response of 1929 to 1933 with the response of 2008, and follow the unemployment numbers year by year.

lessons.title: A President from Illinois
lessons.mainIdea: Barack Obama rose through Chicago organizing and Illinois politics to become the first Black president, and his eight years show how a presidency is shaped by crisis and opposition.
reading: Barack Obama was born in Honolulu in 1961 to a mother from Kansas and a father from Kenya. In 1985 he took a job as a *community organizer* on Chicago's Far South Side, working with churches in Roseland and the Altgeld Gardens housing project in neighborhoods left behind when Wisconsin Steel closed. He went to Harvard Law School, became the first Black president of its law review, and returned to Chicago to practice civil rights law, teach at the University of Chicago and marry Michelle Robinson, who grew up in South Shore. He won a state senate seat from Hyde Park in 1996, lost a 2000 race for Congress, and in 2004 gave a convention speech that made him famous. Illinois elected him to the U.S. Senate that fall. Others had cleared the ground: Harold Washington became Chicago's first Black mayor in 1983, and Carol Moseley Braun of Illinois the first Black woman senator in 1992.

He announced for president in Springfield on February 10, 2007, ran against Hillary Clinton in a long primary that began with a win in Iowa, and faced John McCain in the fall. The financial crash in September 2008 turned the race toward the economy. Obama won about fifty-three percent of the vote and 365 electoral votes, with record turnout among young and Black voters, and celebrated in Grant Park. Twelve weeks later he took office with the economy losing hundreds of thousands of jobs a month.

His first two years produced the *stimulus*, the auto rescue, the Dodd-Frank financial rules and, in March 2010, the *Affordable Care Act*, which required most Americans to carry health insurance, expanded Medicaid and barred insurers from refusing people with existing conditions; by 2016 about twenty million more people had coverage. Every Republican in Congress voted against it. In the 2010 *midterm election* Democrats lost sixty-three House seats, and the rest of the presidency was a struggle with a divided Congress over budgets and debt. Abroad, Obama ended combat in Iraq, expanded drone strikes, ordered the raid that killed bin Laden and signed a climate agreement in Paris in 2015. He won re-election over Mitt Romney in 2012. In 2015 the Supreme Court recognized same-sex marriage nationwide. In 2016 the Senate refused for nearly a year to consider his Supreme Court nominee.

Judging a presidency this recent is hard, and historians know it. Supporters point to the recovery, the health law and the symbolism of the first Black president; critics on the right cite debt and regulation, and critics on the left cite deportations, drone strikes and unprosecuted bankers. Under the *Presidential Records Act*, his papers belong to the public and are opening in stages; the Obama Presidential Center in Jackson Park, a few miles from where he organized, will house exhibits while the records themselves are digital. The ranking will change as the files open, as it did for Truman and Reagan.

lessons.title: Polarization, Screens and a Pandemic
lessons.mainIdea: Since about 2010 American politics has grown more polarized, social media has changed how people learn and argue, and the COVID-19 pandemic tested government and trust at the same time.
reading: *Polarization* means the two parties moving apart. The evidence is in the numbers. In 1994 about one voter in five held a very unfavorable view of the other party; by 2022 more than half did. Votes in Congress fall along party lines far more often than in the 1970s. Explanations compete: the sorting of conservatives into one party and liberals into the other, primaries that reward the loudest candidates, safe districts, and cable news. In 2016 Donald Trump won the presidency in the Electoral College while losing the popular vote. In 2020 Joe Biden defeated him; Trump's claims of a stolen election lost in more than sixty court cases, and on January 6, 2021, a crowd of his supporters stormed the Capitol to stop the count. The House impeached Trump twice; the Senate acquitted him both times. In 2024 he won a second, non-consecutive term.

The screens changed in the middle of this. Facebook opened to the public in 2006, the iPhone arrived in 2007, and within a decade most Americans carried a feed in their pocket. Platforms make money from attention, so an *algorithm* chooses what each person sees, favoring posts that get a reaction. Researchers disagree about how much this drives polarization; some studies find feeds mostly confirm what people already think, others find real effects on anger and *misinformation*. A Senate committee found that a Russian agency ran fake American accounts during the 2016 campaign. Doctors debate the effect on teenagers' mental health. What is not in dispute is that the way most people first learn about an event changed more between 2005 and 2015 than in the previous fifty years.

Then a virus arrived. The second known American case of COVID-19 was a Chicago woman, confirmed in January 2020. On March 11 the World Health Organization declared a *pandemic*; on March 21 Illinois ordered residents to stay home, and schools went online. Unemployment hit nearly fifteen percent in April 2020, the highest since the Depression, and Congress passed a rescue package of about two trillion dollars. On May 25 a Minneapolis police officer killed George Floyd, and protests filled cities including Chicago. Vaccines, developed in under a year, were authorized in December 2020. By 2023 more than a million Americans had died, with deaths falling unevenly by age, race, income and region. Masks and vaccines became partisan markers, and students lost months of learning. Trust in institutions, already low, fell further for many.

These are events you or your family lived through, which makes them hard to see as history. Claims about them contradict one another, and some of the people who made those claims are still making them. One tool is the count of *excess deaths*, the number of people who died beyond what would be expected in a normal year, which cuts through arguments about labels on death certificates. Another is to ask what a historian in 2075 would need: the emails, the school board recordings, the texts between friends, the memory of the empty expressway. Most of that will vanish unless someone saves it.

lessons.title: Writing History While It Happens
lessons.mainIdea: The recent past is the hardest history to write because the sources are incomplete, the outcomes unknown and the historian is a participant, so historians use rules to keep themselves honest.
reading: Harry Truman left office in 1953 with one of the lowest approval ratings ever recorded; historians now rank him among the better presidents. Reagan was dismissed by many scholars in 1989 and reassessed after his diaries and letters were published. Distance changes the view, and so do the records. Under the Presidential Records Act, a president's papers go to the National Archives and open in stages, with the most sensitive files closed for twelve years or more, and classified documents reviewed after twenty-five. Since the 1990s most of those records are *born-digital*: emails, texts, drafts saved over drafts. A tweet can be deleted; a web page can change. The Internet Archive has saved copies of pages since 1996, but only some of them.

Historians working close to the present follow rules. Source every claim: who said it, when, and what did they want. *Corroborate*: find a second, independent record before believing the first. Separate journalism, the first draft, from history, which waits for the drafts underneath. Watch for *hindsight*, the trap of judging a 2003 decision by what was learned in 2004. Watch for *presentism*, judging the past by today's values without first understanding its own. And count the silent: the warehouse worker in 2020 who left no essay, the family in 1980 whose mill closed, the grandmother who watched Watergate on a black-and-white set. Oral history projects, including ones at Chicago museums and libraries, exist to record them before they are gone.

The chapter's own events show how interpretations move. In 1974 Watergate seemed to prove the system worked; a year later the Church Committee showed how much of the system had failed unseen. In 2008 the crash was blamed on greedy borrowers, then on greedy banks, then, by a federal commission, on regulators who looked away; the arguments continue with better data. In 2020 the pandemic's toll was fought over daily; the excess-death counts settled some of it, and more will be settled when hospital and government records open. None of these stories is finished. Each got clearer as evidence arrived and as the people writing it were no longer the people living it.

That makes you a *primary source*. What you keep from this year, a screenshot, a diary, a recording of a grandparent describing a gas line in 1979 or a classroom on September 11, 2001, or an empty street in March 2020, is what a historian will have. The next chapter of this course asks you to choose a question about your own place and pursue it through evidence. This chapter's lesson is the starting rule: the recent past is not yet history, but it is already evidence, and someone has to save it.
